text: Ivan Karlović (c. 1485 – 9 August 1531), also known as Johannes Torquatus in Latin, was the Count of Krbava and the last male descendant of the Kurjaković family from the noble Gusić tribe. Born in Udbina as the son of Karlo Kurjaković and Dorothea Frankopan, he inherited vast estates including the županijas of Krbava, Odorje, Hotuča, Lapac, part of Lika, and several fortified cities after his father's death in 1493. He held the position of Ban of Croatia twice: from 1521 to 1524 and again from 1527 to 1531, and participated in the 1527 Election in Cetin as one of the leading Croatian magnates. During the Hundred Years' Croatian–Ottoman War, he actively resisted Ottoman expansion, engaging in military actions such as defeating an Ottoman army near Gradac in 1500 and fighting against them in Bosnia. He supported Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, during the Hungarian succession crisis in 1506 and held townships like Mutnik and Belaj (today Bilaj) between 1505 and 1509. In 1508, he temporarily fought against Maximilian I’s army in the Venetian hinterland and defended Mutnik from Croatian noblemen, possibly with Ottoman assistance. From 1509 to 1524, he entered into multiple Condottieri contracts with the Republic of Venice to defend its Dalmatian estates, though he refused to participate in a 1510 campaign to free Dalmatia from Venetian control due to financial constraints. In 1513, as Vice-Ban and Captain of Croatia and Dalmatia (1512–1513), he fought in the Battle of Dubica alongside Petar Berislavić and other nobles. In 1514, Ottoman raids targeted his estates in Krbava and Lika, and in 1519, his envoy Stjepan Posedarski delivered an anti-Ottoman speech to Pope Leo X, pleading for help in defense of faith, freedom, and survival. After Petar Berislavić’s death in 1520, Karlović found his severed head and body at Plješivica and had them transported to Bihać and then Veszprem. In 1521, he attempted to negotiate with the Ottomans unsuccessfully and was named Ban of Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia, but failed to prevent the fall of Knin, Skradin, and Ostrovica Fortress. Despite receiving military and financial aid from Archduke Ferdinand I, he resigned as Ban in 1524 due to financial strain and lack of noble support. In December 1526, he participated in the Croatian Election in Cetin, where Croatian nobility elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg as king to counter Ottoman threats, a move that occurred amid a civil war involving John Zápolya. In 1527, he was reappointed Ban and remained in office until his death in 1531, during which he lost key forts such as Obrovac, Udbina, Komić, and Mrsinj-grad, and received substitute estates in Turopolje—Medvedgrad, Lukavec, and Rakovec—from Ferdinand I. In 1528, he led a Croatian army reinforced by Carniolan forces to defeat thousands of Ottoman troops near Belaj, and in 1529, he helped during the Siege of Vienna. He died on 9 August 1531 in Medvedgrad and was buried in the Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Remete, Zagreb, under the great altar. According to the inheritance contract with Nikola III Zrinski, who married his sister Jelena Kurjaković, his estates passed to the Zrinski family due to having no descendants married to the niece of cardinal Tamás Bakócz. He owned 22 forts and cities across three županijas and two župas, including Udbina, Krbava, Kurjak-grad, Turan, Počitelj, Podlapčec, Mrsinj-grad, Lovinac, Gradac, Novigrad, Zvonigrad, Zelengrad, Kličevac, Bag, Obrovac, and Stari Obrovac. His sister Jelena was the mother of Nikola IV Zrinski, future Ban of Croatia and hero of Szigetvár. His nephews, Nikola and Ivan Zrinski, inscribed on his tombstone in 1541: "Sepultus genere Spectabilis militiaque praeditus magnificus dominus Torquatus, comes Corbaviae regnorumque Croatiae et Sclavoniae banus mole sub hac tegitur," which, along with the coat of arms, was later lost. A 16th-century Glagolithic document described the coat of arms as a goose on a shield with the letters I. C. (Joannes Caroli), and Samuel Timon (1736) and Károly Wagner (1802) described it, though their accounts were influenced by 17th-century armorials like Opus Insignium Armorumque (1687–1688) by Johann Weikhard von Valvasor. In folk tradition, ruined towns like Komić, Kozja Draga, and Mazin are still called Karlovića dvori ("Karlović's palaces"). Karlović is the central figure in Fran Binički’s novel Ivan Hrvaćanin (1926) and is remembered in folk poetry, including bugarštica such as "Kad se Ivan Karlović vjerio za kćer kralja Budimskoga," among Molise Croats in Southern Italy, Burgenland Croats in Austria, and Bosniaks, likely descendants of his former subjects. He is referred to in various forms such as Ivan or Jivan Karlović, Ive Karlovićev, Ivan Dovice, did Karlović, Karlo Vića, and Ivan Hrvaćanin. In Molise, fragmented versions of songs in Shtokavian-Chakavian with Ikavian accent and longer Chakavian versions with Ekavian-Ikavian accent are preserved. He is generally portrayed as a noble and tireless warrior against the Ottomans, though in Molise he is negatively depicted as feared by girls picking flowers in meadows, reflecting a folk theme where hero identity is less important and linked to fear and danger during Ottoman conquests, indicating the community’s migration and ethnic identity. Due to the loss of most personal holdings and the biblical reference to Job on his tombstone, he is sometimes called "Job of Croatia."
